transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Morales (Redwood SE), Ethan Walker (CTO - Oculus AI), Priya Shah (ML Eng), Marco Diaz (Infra Lead), Tara Li (Product)

Summary (auto-gen, edited inline):
Deep technical review of long-context (128k+) serving options, focusing on hybrid pipeline that combines prefix streaming, chunked attention, and persistent KV tiers across Redwood Dedicated + on-prem. Discussed latency SLOs, batching windows, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem integration constraints. Agreed to run Redwood 128k runbook and share architecture diagram + security pack.

Topics: long-context architecture, KV caching tiers, batching/latency, quantization profiling, VPC/on-prem deployment, monitoring and rollouts

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Samir: All right hey everyone thanks for joining on short notice. this is Samir from Redwood AE, and I'm here with Lena, our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Ethan: Good thanks, bit of a tight day but ready.
[00:08] Lena: Hi all, I know you sent over the prompt distro earlier, thanks Ethan, that was helpful. we'll dig into the worst-case long docs — 128k plus scenarios — and talk architecture options.
[00:18] Priya: Quick note: our primary concern is p95 latency under 5s for our note-summarization flow that zips through a 150k token document, and we also need strict data residency for some customers.
[00:28] Marco: and we want to avoid hitting external endpoints for the sensitive bits, so on-prem or VPC private lanes are must-haves.
[00:33] Samir: Totally — Redwood Dedicated + Private can be combined. We'll sketch a hybrid pipeline where the heavyweight KV and persistent chunk store runs on your VPC or on-prem nodes and the fast path is on Redwood dedicated GPUs in the same region.

[00:50] [Samir] Quick caveat: I might mis-say some acronyms, transcriber sometimes flips K V cache into K-V chache — apologies.

[01:00] Lena: Let's start with how we treat a 128k+ request. We generally split into three stages: prefix streaming, chunked encoding + KV lookups, and final decode/attention with sparse windowing. For Oculus you probably want persistent KV tiers: hot KV in RAM on dedicated infer nodes, warm KV on your on-prem side for long-term context, and a cold chunk store in object storage.
[01:28] Ethan: Wait, can you explain the difference between "hot" and "warm" KV in practice? like what lives where?
[01:35] Lena: Sure. Hot is the working KV cache that the runtime keeps in GPU RAM for immediate reuse — fast lookups, reduced token generation. Warm is a remote but low-latency store, e.g., your VPC-hosted Redis or a memory-optimized instance, we prefetch segments into hot when we see locality. Cold is S3/GCS for archive and on-demand fetch.
[01:52] Priya: For our workloads we see locality spikes — some documents revisit the same sections, so caching will help. but the tricky bit is sequence lengths vary a lot.
[01:59] Marco: latency concerns — if we prefetch too much we blow memory, if too little we do many RPC hops.

[02:08] Lena: Exactly. That's where adaptive prefetch policies and eviction heuristics come in. Redwood supports cost-aware prefetch: we look at token reuse probability, token age, and request SLA to decide how much to promote from warm to hot.
[02:22] Ethan: How deterministic is that? we need to ensure p99 doesn't spike when one big document hits.
[02:28] Lena: We have soft guarantees. For strict cases you can pin documents to a dedicated node pool or run a local on-prem inference replica for that tenant. For p99 control we recommend horizontal sharding of the KV keyspace and request routing by tenant to avoid thundering herds.

[02:45] [03:00] Samir: Quick interjection — we also saw this in the 128k benchmarks: continuous batching helps throughput but hurts latency tail if not tuned. So it's a balance: small batching windows for low-latency routes, larger windows for throughput routes.

[03:20] Priya: Could you share the numbers? like p95/p99 tradeoffs as we increase batch windows?
[03:26] Lena: Yes, I have a quick summary. On our Dedicated profile with A100 equiv: 1) single-request (no batch) p95 ~ 1.2s token response but throughput low; 2) 20–50ms batching window p95 still under 2s, p99 around 3.5s for heavy 128k flows; 3) 200ms windows pushed throughput up 3x but p99 spiked to 6–8s. Those are ballpark — we'll share the spreadsheet.

[03:55] Marco: Those batch numbers assume KV hits are high, right? What happens when there are a lot of cold reads?
[04:00] Lena: If cold reads dominate, you pay RPC penalty. In that case we suggest a hybrid prefetch that primes KV for the first 2–3 chunks on initial open, then go lazy. Also, we can use block-level checksums in metadata to quickly decide if a chunk is unchanged to avoid re-transfers.

[04:17] Ethan: On quantization — we heard quantization can lower memory footprint but increase decoding time unpredictably. how does Redwood handle quantized kernels for large contexts?
[04:26] Lena: Great question. Redwood's runtime picks kernels based on seq len and quant profile. For 8-bit dynamic quant we get ~2–2.5x memory reduction with modest CPU overhead. But some quant kernels aren't friendly to very long KV cache iterations — they add jitter. For deterministic low-tail latency, we recommend mixed approach: run attr-heavy sections with FP16 and less-critical sections quantized, or use quant profiles tuned during our optimize tool.

[04:52] Priya: So you'd suggest hybrid quant per segment? that sounds complex to orchestrate.
[04:56] Lena: It's orchestrated by the runtime: segments are profiled during dry runs and assigned a quant profile. You can override with per-tenant policies. The key is to test with your real prompt distribution.

[05:10] Samir: Also note that quantization affects kernel selection and batching behavior. Some batched kernels only exist for FP16 paths, so if you mix you might lose some batching efficiency. That's in the tradeoff spreadsheet.

[05:25] [05:30] Marco: About attention optimizations — we use chunked attention and sometimes sliding-window. can you walk through Redwood's sparse strategies for 128k?
[05:36] Lena: Sure. We support several modes: global-local hybrid (global tokens routed to full attention, local tokens use sliding windows), rotary-based chunking with sparse inter-chunk attention, and strided sparse attention. For 128k, we often do hierarchical chunking: inner chunks of 2k with local attention, plus periodic global tokens at 16k cadence that get routed through a smaller full-attn layer. That reduces compute from O(N^2) to approx O(N * chunk_size).

[06:06] Priya: Does that change generation coherence? our summaries need cross-document references.
[06:10] Lena: There's a tradeoff: the global token cadence must be dense enough to capture cross-chunk coref. We recommend running evals with a held-out set that has cross-chunk references and tuning global cadence until Rouge/BLEU/our eval metrics stabilize.

[06:24] Ethan: For the hybrid deployment we discussed — if the cold store is on-prem and hot nodes are Redwood Dedicated — what's the network pattern? do we see many synchronous calls from the GPU nodes to our VPC?
[06:35] Lena: In the conservative setup yes: hot node will synchronously fetch on misses. To lower tail latency we recommend two things: 1) frontload prefetch for the first N chunks as part of request admission; 2) colocate warm KV in a peered VPC in the same region, or use dedicated interconnects. We also support gRPC multiplexing and parallel chunk fetch so the runtime can pipeline fetch + decode.

[07:02] Marco: For compliance we need audit logs of every fetch and a replayable trace. Is that available?
[07:07] Samir: Yes, Redwood Private includes per-request audit logs, tracing hooks, and a lineage artifact. We can push to your SIEM or collect in S3. We'll include the policy mapping in the security pack.

[07:18] Priya: One more thing — cost. If we pin a tenant to a dedicated node pool for p99 control, what's the cost ballpark?
[07:24] Samir: Depends on GPU sku and commit. For a small pilot (2 nodes with A100 equiv) expect $Xk/month; we'll produce a detailed estimate based on your throughput numbers. I'll add that as action item.

[07:36] [07:40] Lena: There was a question earlier on how the runtime handles KV eviction under memory pressure — short answer: it uses LRU with usage-weighting by token reuse and an async writeback to warm tier. We also support snapshotting of KV shards for fast warm restarts.

[07:55] Ethan: Can we see a short demo of the runbook, like warmup + prefetch pattern?
[07:59] Lena: I can show a local repro flow — do you want the recorded commands?
[08:04] Tara: Yes please — we want to hand off to infra afterwards.

[08:07] [Demo portion - Lena screenshared command snippets briefly, not fully captured by transcript]
[08:15] Lena: (paraphrasing) example run: redwood-run --model x-large --kv-tier warm:redis://oculus-warm:6379 --prefetch 3 --batch-window-ms 50 --quant-profile mixed-8fp16. That will simulate a 128k doc broken into 2k chunks with prefetch of 3 chunks.

[08:38] Marco: That CLI helps. Is that the same code path when we do on-prem?
[08:42] Lena: The same runtime; on-prem you deploy the runtime with the private control plane. The difference is the KV endpoints and storage. We'll help with Helm charts.

[08:50] Ethan: About monitoring — we need token-level cost, per-route latency, and KV hit/miss dashboards. is that built in?
[08:56] Samir: Redwood Console has per-route dashboards, KV hit/miss counters, token-cost breakdown, and trace linking. We'll give you dashboard templates you can import.

[09:06] Priya: Are there any gotchas for very long context with streaming responses? some models drop earlier context when streaming.
[09:12] Lena: Streaming plus long-context requires careful KV cursor management. We recommend final decode happens only after core prefix streaming and key KV priming. Also watch for tokenization chunk boundaries — off-by-one token splits can cause drift; our runtime aligns chunks on sentence boundaries when possible.

[09:30] Ethan: Can you summarize recommended pilot architecture?
[09:33] Samir: Sure. Pilot: 1) Redwood Dedicated infer pool in same region for hot compute; 2) Oculus-managed VPC warm-KV cluster (memory-optimized) with peering; 3) Cold chunk store in your object storage; 4) small on-prem replica for the most-sensitive tenant data (air-gapped) with private control plane; 5) initial batch window 50ms, prefetch 3, quant-profile mixed-8fp16 for first pass; 6) monitoring + trace, and canary rollout policy.

[09:58] Marco: That sounds workable. timeline?
[10:00] Samir: We propose 2-week pilot prep, 1-week run, results and tuning week after. So kickoff next week if you want.

[10:09] Priya: We'll need the security pack before kickoff.

[10:12] Samir: Yes — I'll send SOC2/ISO docs and the VPC checklist.

[10:16] Lena: Action items — I'll run the dedicated 128k runbook and capture the p95/p99 numbers with the exact flags we discussed and send the log + spreadsheet.

[10:24] Ethan: Great. we'll pull together prompt samples and internal compliance gating list.

[10:29] Samir: Ok let's recap the next steps. I'll list them in the follow-up email. Quick note: docs and benchmark spreadsheet links: Link: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/128k-hybrid (we'll attach the real spreadsheet). Security pack link placeholder: https://redwood.example/security-pack

[10:46] Tara: Thanks everyone. good session.
[10:49] Samir: Thanks all, we'll follow up.

[END]
